# THE ART OF EFFORT: Philosophy and Intellectual Overcoming

The video combines mythology and philosophy to respond to what makes a life successful. It goes through the choice of Ulysses on the island of Calipso, the eudaimonia of Aristotle and the firmness that the video connects to Nietzsche, and ends in the brio: the refusal to be defeated by a difficult text.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on November 13, 2026 (6 min 21 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tt2XRKbusbs

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## The question: what makes a life successful

The video proposes to refuse passive comfort and accept intellectual friction as a way to find a purpose [00:14]. The question that guides analysis is the oldest of all: what really matters in life [00:30].

## Ulysses and the island of Calipso

Na *Odyssey*, from Homer, Ulysses is stuck on an island with the goddess Calipso [00:48]. The island has all the comfort, but every night he goes to the beach crying of homesickness [01:06].

Calipso offers him immortality, and Ulysses refuses [01:17]. He prefers to age and die, provided it is in Ithaca, his land [01:25]. The video summarizes the choice as follows: Better to be a mortal man in the right place than a god in the wrong place [01:34]. There is no real success in spending life standing where the tide left us [01:41].

## Aristotle's Eudaimony

Around 350 B.C., Aristotle defined the purpose of life, and for him success has no relation to passive comfort [01:51]. The word he uses is *idaimony*: the active realization of their own talents, the happiness that comes from seeking excellence and developing their own nature altogether [02:04].

The video compares this to a tree change on fertile soil, which needs to create roots, grow to maximum height and bear fruit [02:25]. With people it is the same: there is an ethical commitment not to atrophy growth itself and to go as far as possible with the resources and intelligence we already have [02:36].

## The firmness: after finding out, do not back down

The third point part of a phrase of popular wisdom: "It takes as long as it takes to realize what you want of existence, but when you realize it, do not retreat on any pretext" [02:47]. Discovering the purpose requires patience; defending the purpose requires an almost stubborn conviction [02:58].

For the video, the phrase echoes Nietzsche's philosophy, mainly in *So spoke Zarathustra*: when a person understands who he is, he advances, and does not go back nor to take impulse [03:07]. The world will always put obstacles and voices that try to dissuade those who seek something big, and against this friction retreat is not an option [03:35].

## The brio test

What sustains this determination is brio: a moral unconformism, a pride that says "I refuse to accept my own ignorance" [03:59]. It is the discipline of not feeding the mind only with superficial information and easy to swallow [04:13].

Improving reasoning wears out, because it forces you to face difficult texts from the front [04:23]. The video gives examples:

- read the ideas of Immanuel Kant until breaking the barrier of understanding [04:30];
- use shame constructively to dissect Pierre Bourdieu's theses by refusing to be less intelligent than the text [04:37];
- remember that Pythagoras, starting almost from scratch, unveiled the relationships of the triangle, and that today, with so much information available, there is no excuse to claim disability [04:50].

Spending an early morning reading 30 times the same difficult paragraph may seem absurd, but the video treats it as a source of pride, and not as punishment [05:04]. It is to look at the text and say, "I will never be defeated by a mere set of words" [05:20].

## The Art of Effort

The conclusion is that excellence belongs to those who reject the shallow waters and the misleading ease of the island of Calipso [05:30]. It belongs to those who discover their own purpose, take control of their own intelligence and face intellectual friction with brio [05:41]. Everything depends on sustaining the discipline of effort to the end [05:51].

The video closes with a question for the viewer: what is the intellectual barrier that will not defeat us today [05:54]?

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is eudaimonia?

It is the term Aristotle uses for the ultimate purpose of life: the active realization of his own talents, the happiness that comes from seeking excellence [02:04].

### Why does Ulysses refuse immortality?

Because he would rather be mortal in his own land, Ithaca, than immortal in the wrong place [01:25].

### What does the video call brio?

A moral unconformism, the pride of refusing to accept ignorance itself in the face of a text or a difficult idea [03:59].

## About the video

Have you ever felt like giving up when facing a difficult book or an intellectual challenge? In a world dominated by superficial content and ready answers, true mental strength is becoming a rarity.

In this explanatory video, we unite great lessons from classical mythology and Western philosophy to answer two fundamental questions: **What makes a truly good life?** and **how to develop the intellectual musculature to never back away from the difficult?**

Learn from the wise choice of Ulysses by refusing immortality on the island of Calipso to return to its right place (Itaca), understand the quest for excellence (*idaimony*) in Aristotle and discover Nietzsche's unwavering determination. Finally, face the test of **brio** — the unconformism that prevents us from accepting cognitive defeat in the face of dense texts such as those of Kant and Bourdieu.

Put blood in your veins, refuse mediocrity and discover the power of deliberate effort.

* **Friedrich Nietzsche** – *So spoke Zarathustra* (Firing and perseverance)
* **Immanuel Kant** – *Grounds for Metaphysics of Customs* (Discipline of thought)
* **Pierre Bourdieu** – *The Production of Belief* (Sociology and intellectual overcoming)
